name: Choguita Rarámuri
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Caballero, Gabriela (2022). A grammar of Choguita Rarámuri. Comprehensive Grammar Library 5. Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.7189161 (CC BY).
catalog_locator: §2.1.2 'Stress, tone and prosodic structure', pp. 43-44; ch. 5 'Stress', §5.1 pp. 134-135; §5.3 and rule (17) p. 151; §5.4 'Initial three-syllable stress window' pp. 161-168; weight-insensitivity stated ch. 11 pp. 404, 407 (pp. 422, 425).
catalog_quote: [p. 43] Stress in Choguita Rarámuri is lexically contrastive and assigned to the first, second or third syllable within an initial three-syllable window. Stress in inflected words is determined by the stress properties of both roots and suffixes: roots are stressed or unstressed (with fixed or shifting stress across paradigms, respectively), while suffixes are stress-shifting or stress-neutral. [p. 134] ... stress is underlyingly present for at least some morphemes in this language, and can create lexical contrasts. ... a. ˈmúri ‘basket’, ‘canasta’ b. muˈrí ‘turtle’, ‘tortuga’ ... the stress system of Choguita Rarámuri is in part phonologically determined and partly morphologically-conditioned, as attested in other lexical stress systems. [p. 135] There is no evidence for secondary stress in Choguita Rarámuri. ... Stress is left-aligned and assigned in the first (2a), second (2b–c) or third (2d–e) syllable of the word. [p. 151] Lexical stress in roots blocks morphologically-conditioned stress shifts; stress in these cases will be fixed on the first, second or third syllable, regardless of what suffixes are attached. ... In words containing unstressed roots and stress-neutral suffix, stress will be assigned by default on the second syllable of the root or the only syllable of monosyllabic roots. ... stress shifts rightward. [p. 407] Given that there is no role for contrastive vowel length in stress assignment, this is a weight-insensitive iambic system.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: cent2131 (Central Tarahumara = Choguita Rarámuri, Guachochi municipality, 'Central' dialect area per Caballero et al. 2022 p. 2) is not in the catalog. All four target items are by Gabriela Caballero and are about word stress in this variety. Read in full: (a) Caballero 2005 ROA-706 manuscript (downloaded from roa.rutgers.edu, 27 pp.): mixed lexical/default stress system, initial trisyllabic window, no secondary stress, default 2nd-syllable stem stress with weak suffixes and 3rd-syllable with strong suffixes (p. 15); (b) Caballero, Chai & Garellek 2022 OUP chapter (author preprint downloaded from Yuan Chai's github page): stress lexically contrastive, initial three-syllable window, non-iterative (p. 3), chapter otherwise about tone f0/voice quality and intonation; (c) not in the target list but the authoritative source: Caballero 2022 A grammar of Choguita Rarámuri (LangSci Press, open access; copy already held by the project in our check tree), §2.1.2 p. 43 and ch. 5 pp. 133-166. Not obtainable: Caballero 2011 Linguistics (De Gruyter, closed, abstract not retrievable) and Caballero & Carroll 2015 IJAL (closed; abstract saved from Semantic Scholar) — both medium priority only, since the 2022 grammar covers and cites them. The 2008 UC Berkeley dissertation is linked from the author's site only via a login-gated Google Drive link and eScholarship search returned nothing fetchable. Recommended coding for a new catalog record: lexical stress, initial three-syllable window, left-aligned, no secondary stress, deciding source Caballero 2022 grammar p. 43.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs like ˈmúri 'basket' vs muˈrí 'turtle') and is confined to an initial three-syllable window: it falls on the first, second or third syllable of the word, never further right. Roots are either stressed (fixed stress in the 1st or 2nd syllable across paradigms) or unstressed; unstressed roots get default stress on their second syllable (or the only syllable of a monosyllabic root) when combined with stress-neutral suffixes, and stress shifts one syllable rightward onto a stress-shifting suffix (rule (17), p. 151). A three-way lexical tone contrast (HL, L, H) is realized only on the stressed syllable. Acoustic cues are primarily intensity and duration; unstressed vowels reduce/delete (§5.2).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'There is no evidence for secondary stress in Choguita Rarámuri. That is, there is no impressionistic evidence of rhythmic prominence' (p. 135); the 2022 preprint calls the system non-iterative.
new_statements.exceptions: Stressed roots block morphological stress shifts; stress shift alone can encode imperative, denominalization and applicative categories (chs. 9, 11); the three-syllable window is enforced in compounds and multiply suffixed words, and Spanish loanwords whose source stress lies outside the window are truncated to keep it inside (§7.3); fourth-syllable stress is unattested.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prosodic word), for both bare/citation forms and inflected words; window counted from the left edge of the word. Lexical tone is dependent on stress; the language is described as a stress-accent language with lexical tone (hybrid), not as a tone language.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Choguita Rarámuri (community of Choguita, municipality of Guachochi, Chihuahua). Caballero 2022 §1.1.2.1 (p. 6) places it in Ethnologue's Central Tarahumara [tar] (= Glottolog cent2131), in a transitional area between the Central and Northern dialects of Valiñas' (2001)/INALI classification; Glottolog itself files the grammar under cent2131. Caballero's 2005 ROA paper labels the same data 'Central Raramuri'. Note that Brambila 1953 and Lionnet (Norogachi), also filed under cent2131 by Glottolog, are called a 'Northern variety' by Caballero 2022: 12.

new_statements.reading: Lexical (contrastive) word stress, morphologically conditioned, confined to a left-edge three-syllable window (stress on syllable 1, 2 or 3; never further right). One stress per word, no secondary stress (Caballero 2005 p. 3; Caballero, Chai & Garellek 2022 preprint p. 3). Default for lexically unstressed roots: second syllable of the stem with stress-neutral suffixes, third syllable with stress-shifting suffixes (Caballero 2005 p. 15; grammar Table 2.3 p. 43). Correlates: duration and vowel reduction; a separate three-way lexical tone contrast rides on the stressed syllable. on the catalog's classification this is a lexical system with an initial three-syllable window (not quantity-sensitive; no contrastive vowel length).

new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per prosodic word, no secondary stress. Stress is lexical for some roots (minimal pairs by stress position); roots are stressed or unstressed and suffixes stress-shifting or stress-neutral. Words with an unstressed root and no stress-shifting suffix take stress on the second root syllable; with a stress-shifting suffix, on the third syllable of the word; lexical root stress blocks these defaults. Stress never falls to the right of the third syllable (initial three-syllable window, left-aligned). Correlates: vowel duration (stressed roughly twice unstressed), unstressed-vowel reduction/deletion, onset augmentation. Derived vowel length plays no role in stress placement (not weight-sensitive).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly none: '(b) There is no secondary stress' (p. 173); 'there is no audible secondary stress' (p. 176).
new_statements.exceptions: Incorporated (body-part incorporation) constructions show a dominant stress pattern deleting inherent stress of the members (p. 174 item i, §4.3.2); imperative final-stem stress shift (§3.4.1.3, §3.5.2.4); in multiply affixed words stress depends on the Stem (root + first suffix) only (item g).
new_statements.identity_note: Work 0 (ELAR 0056 / Caballero 2008 dissertation) describes Choguita Rarámuri (Choguita, municipio de Guachochi, Chihuahua), the catalog's variety, which Caballero places within Ethnologue Central Tarahumara [tar] = cent2131. Work 1 (Hilton 1993) describes the Tarahumara of Samachique, municipio de Guachochi, 'región tarahumara del centro' (p. v), also Central Tarahumara [tar] but a different community from Choguita.

new_statements.quote: [p. viii] ACENTUACIÓN En las palabras tarahumaras presentadas en este vocabulario usamos las mismas reglas de acentuación que se usan en español, así que, cuando el acento cae en la penúltima sílaba no lo marcamos. Hay algunas palabras que llevan dos acentos. [p. v] También hay ciertas variaciones entre las vocales i y e, cuando no están en la sílaba tónica, como en el siguiente ejemplo: quima o quema cobija. [p. 135, §3 Verbos] 2. Los que indican el tiempo futuro quitando el acento de la raíz y agregando el sufijo -méa en las formas singulares y en la tercera persona de plural, y agregando el sufijo -boa o -poa en la primera y segunda persona de plural.
new_statements.translation: [p. viii] ACCENTUATION. For the Tarahumara words in this vocabulary we use the same accentuation rules as in Spanish, so when the stress falls on the penultimate syllable we do not mark it. Some words carry two accents. [p. v] There is also some variation between the vowels i and e when they are not in the stressed syllable, e.g. quima or quema 'blanket'. [p. 135] 2. (The second verb class comprises) those that mark the future by removing the accent from the root and adding the suffix -méa in the singular forms and the third person plural, and -boa or -poa in the first and second person plural.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's lexical, morphologically conditioned stress: stress must be marked per word (not fixed) and a future suffix (-méa) removes root stress, which parallels Caballero's stress-shifting suffixes (Choguita future singular -ma/-méa). The work describes the Samachique (municipio de Guachochi) variety of 'la región tarahumara del centro' = Central Tarahumara [tar], the same Glottolog language as Choguita but a different community; it adds no placement rule, window or default, so it neither refines nor contradicts the Choguita statement. The 'dos acentos' remark is orthographic and is not evidence against Caballero's 'no secondary stress' for Choguita.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The dictionary states no placement rule. It treats stress as a property to be written word by word with Spanish orthographic conventions (penultimate stress unmarked, any other position marked with an acute), i.e. stress position is not predictable from the spelling alone and varies across words (entries show e.g. coná 'sal', chomá 'moco', saté 'arena', boní 'hermano menor' with final stress beside unmarked penultimate forms such as ane, cona-hua); stress interacts with morphology: class-2 verbs lose root stress before the stressed future suffix -méa (a stress-shifting suffix), and unstressed i/e neutralize outside the tonic syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only the orthographic remark 'Hay algunas palabras que llevan dos acentos' (some words carry two written accents), unexplained; no statement about secondary stress as such.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb class 2 (future in -méa/-boa/-poa with loss of root accent) and a subclass with suppletive plural roots; free variation i~e in unstressed syllables; l~r variation word-medially.

Legible fragments: every word has its own accent and compounds may have several; imperatives 'se suele poner el acento en la última'; 'Los futuros de ordinario tienen en la penúltima el acento'; some minimal pairs distinguished by accent. sources.quote: we propose that (i) stress-accent and tone are phonologically distinct systems in Choguita Rarámuri; (ii) stress-accent and tone are independent in terms of their acoustic encoding; (iii) both stress-accent and tone are governed in their distribution and makeup by lexical and morphological conditions; (iv) the tone system features a three-way contrast between HL, L, and M; and (v) lexical tonal contrasts are exclusively realized in stressed syllables—that is, tonal distribution is dependent on stress-accent.
